newsitem.title: THAILAND: Siam Commercial says clients hit harder than banks.
newsitem.headline: Siam Commercial says clients hit harder than banks.

text.p: Thai commercial banks are less likely to be harmed by foreign exchange losses following the baht's float than their less well-protected customers, a senior bank executive said on Wednesday.
The central bank moved to float the baht in the open market ending months of speculation that an adjustment in the baht regime was looming.
The baht lost around 15-20 percent of its value in offshore markets dropping to 29.10 baht per dollar on Wednesday against around 25.00 baht on Monday.
Legal regulations restricting commercial bank's exposure to currency fluctuations will probably protect the banks from losses on their foreign borrowing, Sataporn said.

"The impact on commercial banks is not likely to be significant as banks always have to take care of these positions, so the impact will probably be on the customers rather than on the banks," said Sataporn Jinachitra, executive vice president at Siam Commercial Bank Plc, one of the country's big four banks.
The bank was checking with its clients to establish which clients had foreign exchange losses on foreign denominated borrowing, he said.
"As of today we don't know who are the losers from the exchange adjustment and there will be some losers. Abrupt changes always bring big adjustments in certain businesss," Sataporn said.
"It is not yet clear what the impact on customers is. Who is hit badly is something that is not clear. I think our credit officers are reviewing that with our customers," he said.
The bank itself may also be facing some small losses on its positions, he added.

"Some banks will make profit, some banks will make a loss. It's basically depends on overnight positions. I think we normally have square positions but basically we were not prepared for the change in exchange rates so there might be some small loss," he said.
"In our bank we don't go for speculation we try to hedge wherever possible so there is no substantial loss but we don't have profit either. We probably have some small loss," he added.
Siam Commercial Bank President and head of the Thai Bankers Associations Olarn Chaiprawat has long warned a baht devaluation would have a harmful impact on the Thai economy.
The effects of the currency adjustment on the economy now remained to be seen, Sataporn said.
"I think in a way it was what the international community expected ... but it remains to be seen whether this will be good for the economy," he said.
"But we are a country that operates an open economy in a globalising world so it's difficult for Thailand to work against international expectations," he added.
